title: Forward Deployed Engineer
subtitle: Field manual: discovery, integration, deployment, client craft

modules.title: The whole job, explained with a bakery

lessons.title: The whole job, explained with a bakery

blocks.text: Start here · no background needed

Think of a clothing factory and a tailor. The factory makes one shirt design for thousands of people. The tailor goes to one customer, measures them, and alters the shirt until it fits. Afterwards the tailor tells the factory which sizes people keep asking for.
A normal software engineer works in the factory. A **Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE)** is the tailor. "Forward deployed" means placed close to the customer, at their office, working on their problem.
Here is a small invented example. Every big-company term used later in this manual shows up in it.

lessons.title: Anand Bakery: four shops, too much wasted bread

blocks.text: Anand Bakery has four shops in one city. Your company sold them billing software last year. The owner calls and says: *"Your software is fine, but I am still throwing away bread every night, and one shop runs out by 6 pm. Can you fix it?"*
You are sent as the FDE. You are not there to sell anything. You are there to make the software they already bought solve this problem.
The five steps you take at the bakery. The small grey word under each box is what an FDE calls that step. The rest of this manual is these five steps at company size.

items: **Listen.** You spend two evenings in the shops. You see that the head baker decides how much to bake from memory, the same amount every day. Saturdays sell out. Tuesdays leave trays of bread.
**Measure.** You count with the owner: about 60 loaves are thrown away each day across the four shops. You agree a goal of 20. Now everyone knows what "fixed" means.

**Gather data.** Sales are in the billing software. How much was baked is in a paper notebook. Bread moved between shops is in a WhatsApp group. The billing software calls a shop "Shop 2" and the notebook calls it "Kothrud". You bring all of it into one table: shop, day, baked, sold, wasted.

**Build small.** For one week you fill a simple sheet by hand each night: for each shop, the average sold on the same weekday over the last four weeks, plus a small extra. The head baker follows the sheet. Waste drops, and the baker asks to keep it.

**Run it daily.** You turn the sheet into a small program inside the billing software. It runs every night, prints a bake slip at 5 am, and sends the owner a message if it fails. You teach the head baker how to adjust the numbers for a festival day. Then you leave, and it keeps working.

blocks.text: Loaves thrown away per day, all four shops. Invented numbers for the example. The result is shown as the number the owner cares about, not as lines of code written.
Why this is FDE work and not ordinary coding

items: Nobody gave you a specification. You found the real problem by watching.
Most of the effort was getting three messy sources into one table, not writing clever code.
You were finished when the bread waste dropped and the baker could run it alone, not when the code compiled.
Back at your company you report: "every bakery customer needs a bake-list feature." That may become part of the product.

blocks.title: Check yourself: at the bakery, what was the metric, and who was the sponsor?
blocks.text: The metric was loaves thrown away per day, with a baseline of 60 and a target of 20. The sponsor was the owner, because the owner pays and wants that number to move.

blocks.title: Check yourself: why fill the sheet by hand for a week before writing a program?
blocks.text: To find out cheaply whether the baker would follow it and whether waste would drop. If the idea had been wrong, you would have lost a week of evenings, not a month of programming.

The tailor from the bakery example. You go to one customer, find what is really wrong, fix it with software, and bring what you learned back to your company. This section says how such a person thinks.

A Forward Deployed Engineer is a software engineer who works inside the customer's problem instead of inside the product roadmap. You sit with the people who use the software, find out what is stopping them, and write whatever code closes the gap: a connector, a pipeline, a data model, a small application, a configuration of your company's platform.

The title was made common by Palantir, which called the role "Delta". It has since spread to data platform, infrastructure and AI companies, because enterprise software rarely works out of the box. The customer's data is messy, their systems are old, and the value only appears once someone connects the product to the real workflow.
A product engineer ships one capability to many customers. An FDE ships many capabilities to one customer, then tells product which of them every customer needs.
The job is a two-way relay. Pain and data come in from the client, working software goes back. Gaps found in the field go to product, and what product generalises returns to every client.
Outcome over output
Nobody at the client cares how many pull requests you merged. They care that late shipments dropped. Tie every week of work to a number the client already tracks.
Bias to a working thing
A rough tool on real data on day five teaches more than a perfect design on day thirty. Show something, watch people use it, then harden it.
Own the whole problem
Access request stuck with IT? That is your problem. The model is right but nobody opens the dashboard? Also yours. There is no "not my layer".
Comfort with mess
You will get half a schema, a contradicting spreadsheet and a deadline. Good FDEs make a reasonable assumption, write it down, and move.
Think in reuse
After you solve it once, ask what part belongs in the product. One-off hacks that never get generalised become a maintenance bill.
Earn trust daily
You are a guest with production access. Do what you said, flag bad news early, and never surprise the client's IT or security team.

rows: Make the product deliver value at this client
Win the deal with demos and proofs of concept
Configure the product to a plan

blocks.title: Check yourself: a client asks for a feature that takes two weeks and helps only them. What do you ask first?
blocks.text: Ask what decision or task it unblocks and what happens today without it. Often a smaller change gets the same result. If it is truly needed, build it in a way that can be lifted into the product later, and tell product about the gap.

blocks.title: Check yourself: why is "the code works" not the finish line?
blocks.text: Because value arrives only when people change how they work. Until an operator trusts the output and uses it in the real process, the engagement has produced nothing the client will renew for.
A doctor on a home visit talks to the patient, examines, treats, and writes notes before leaving. An FDE day has the same four parts: talk to people, look at their data, build, write it down.

No two days match, but the shape repeats. Mornings and late afternoons belong to people. The middle of the day is protected building time. The last half hour is for writing things down, because an FDE who does not write loses the client's context and the product team's attention.
An example day on site, drawn to scale. Block widths are an illustration of a common pattern, not a measurement.

items: **09:00 Stand-up with the client team.** What changed overnight, what is blocked, who you need today.
**09:30 Build.** Pipeline, integration or app work while your head is clear.
**11:30 Sit with a user.** Watch them do the real task. Do not demo. Take notes on where they hesitate.
**12:30 Lunch,** ideally with someone from the client. Half of all useful context arrives here.
**13:15 Build and debug.** Usually a data surprise found in the morning.
**15:15 Stakeholder sync or demo.** Show working software, confirm the next decision.
**16:00 Chase and unblock.** Access requests, firewall rules, a missing column, a security review form.
**17:00 Write.** Site log for the team, and a short note to product on any gap found.
**17:30 Plan tomorrow** and send the client a two-line update.

blocks.text: Illustrative time split by phase. Discovery is mostly conversation. The prototype phase is mostly code and data. Production adds a large share of documentation, tests and handover (5% in the prototype row is unlabelled).
Weekly rhythm

items: Monday: agree the week's single goal with the client lead.
Midweek: an informal demo to real users.
Friday: written status. Done, learned, blocked, next.
Friday: field report to your product team.

Access granted, pending or refused.
Data oddities, with the query that shows them.

blocks.text: Section 3 · basic to intermediate

You need a working amount of four jobs: a programmer who can build it, a plumber who can connect data, a detective who can find the real problem, and a teacher who can explain it. The tables show what each looks like for a beginner and for an expert.
My judgement of the two profiles on a 0 to 5 scale, outer ring is 5. A product engineer goes deeper on code. An FDE needs to be strong on every axis at once.

The FDE profile is wide. You do not need to be the best programmer in the company. You need to be good enough at code that nothing technical blocks you, and far better than a typical engineer at talking to people and working with unclear requirements.
Interviewers test for this width. Expect a coding round, a data or SQL round, a system design round framed around a customer, and a case interview where the problem is vague on purpose.

modules.title: Data integration, the core technical craft

lessons.title: Data integration, the core technical craft

blocks.text: Data integration is plumbing. Each system is a tank with its own pipe size. You connect them so one clean tap gives the answer. At the bakery it was billing export plus notebook plus WhatsApp into one table. A **pipeline** is the set of steps that does this copying and cleaning on a schedule.

Most engagements are won or lost on data. The client has the information they need, spread over systems that were never designed to talk to each other. Your job is to bring it into one place, clean it, and shape it into objects the business recognises.

The layered flow you will rebuild at almost every client. Keeping an untouched raw copy lets you fix a cleaning mistake without asking the client to resend data. The dashed arrow is what separates an operational tool from a report.
Batch vs CDC vs streaming

**Batch** copies on a schedule and is the right default. **Change data capture** reads the database log and sends only changed rows, with low load on the source. **Streaming** handles events as they occur. Pick the slowest option that still meets the decision's deadline.
Idempotency
Running the same load twice must give the same result. Use a stable key and `MERGE` or upsert instead of blind inserts. This makes retries and backfills safe.
Schema drift
Source teams rename and add columns without telling you. Detect it at ingest, fail loudly on a breaking change, and pass through additive changes.
Data contracts
A written agreement with the source owner: columns, types, freshness, who to call. It turns "the feed broke" from your surprise into their alert.
Quality checks
Row counts against yesterday, null rates on key columns, uniqueness of keys, freshness, valid ranges. Block the pipeline on a failed critical check.
Lineage
For any number on screen, you can name the tables and source rows behind it. When a user says "this is wrong", lineage is how you answer in minutes.
The same customer, product or site appears under different names and IDs in each system. Until you match them, joins silently drop rows. This is the single most common hidden problem in client data.
Blocking keeps the comparison count manageable. The human review step uses the client's knowledge and builds their trust in the result.

blocks.code:
-- Match warehouse sites between the WMS and the transport system.
-- Pass 1: exact match on a cleaned postcode + first word of the name.
WITH wms AS (
  SELECT site_id,
         UPPER(REPLACE(postcode, ' ', ''))        AS pc,
         UPPER(SPLIT_PART(TRIM(site_name), ' ', 1)) AS name_key
  FROM raw_wms.sites
),
tms AS (
  SELECT depot_code,
         UPPER(REPLACE(zip, ' ', ''))               AS pc,
         UPPER(SPLIT_PART(TRIM(depot_name), ' ', 1)) AS name_key
  FROM raw_tms.depots
)
SELECT w.site_id, t.depot_code, 'postcode+name' AS match_rule
FROM wms w
JOIN tms t ON t.pc = w.pc AND t.name_key = w.name_key;
-- Anything left unmatched goes to a review sheet for the ops lead.

blocks.text: Run on PostgreSQL 16 with three sample sites. Leeds and Hull matched. "Derby Hub" against "East Mids" did not, so it goes to the review sheet.

Users do not think in tables. They think in shipments, trucks, customers and orders. Model those as objects with properties, links between them, and actions people can take on them. Some platforms call this layer an ontology. When the model matches the client's vocabulary, every app, alert and AI assistant built on it is easier to explain.

blocks.title: Check yourself: a nightly join suddenly returns 8% fewer rows. Where do you look?
blocks.text: Compare row counts per layer to find where the drop begins. Then check the join keys: a format change in one source (leading zeros, case, a new ID scheme) is the usual cause. Check for late-arriving data and for a failed upstream load that left a partial table.

blocks.title: Check yourself: when would you refuse to build a streaming pipeline?
blocks.text: When the decision it feeds is made hourly or daily. Streaming costs more to build and to run, and is harder to backfill. If the dispatcher plans routes once each morning, a batch at 05:00 is correct.

Where does the software live? Three choices. A restaurant: customers send their data to your kitchen (vendor cloud). A private chef: you cook in the customer's kitchen (their cloud account). A locked kitchen with no phone: you bring everything with you (air-gapped). Then: who has keys, and what happens when something burns.

Enterprise clients decide where your software runs, and the answer changes how you ship, debug and upgrade. Learn all three patterns. The stricter the environment, the more your release process has to work without you being able to see it.

What moves between the three is where the platform box sits and who can reach it. In the air-gapped case you cannot pull an image or read a log remotely, so releases ship as tested offline bundles with their own diagnostics.
Security you will be asked about in week one

items: **SSO:** users log in with the client's identity provider through SAML or OIDC.
**Least privilege:** a read-only service account per source, scoped to the tables you need.
**Permissions on data:** role-based access, plus row and column rules for sensitive fields.
**Encryption** in transit and at rest, and secrets in a vault, never in code.
**Audit log:** who saw or changed what.
**Personal data:** know where it is, mask what is not needed.

blocks.text: What "production" means

items: Runs without you: scheduled, monitored, alerting a named owner.
Tested: unit tests on logic, data checks on every run.
Recoverable: every release can be rolled back, every load re-run.
Documented: a runbook for the five most likely failures.
Handed over: a client engineer has fixed a staged failure alone.
Measured: the outcome metric is on a dashboard the sponsor reads.

blocks.text: Communicate before you diagnose. A client forgives an outage they heard about from you. They do not forgive finding a wrong number themselves.

A good contractor renovating a house asks what bothers the family, agrees in writing what is included, shows a sample wall, finishes the job, and hands over the keys with instructions. Client craft is the same steps with software.
The engagement lifecycle. Durations are typical ranges. Do not start a phase until the previous gate is met, or you will build the wrong thing well.
Discovery questions that work

items: "Walk me through the last time this went wrong."
"What do you do right after you look at this report?"
"Which spreadsheet do you keep that IT does not know about?"
"If this were fixed, what number would move, and who reports it?"
"What have you tried before, and why did it stop?"
"Who would be unhappy if we changed this?"

blocks.text: A scope statement in five lines

items: **User:** who uses it, by job title.
**Decision:** the one decision it improves.
**Metric:** the number, its baseline and the target.
**Data:** the sources needed, and their owners.
**Out of scope:** what you will not do in this phase.

blocks.text: Stakeholder map for the scenario in section 7. Security and IT have low interest and high influence, which is why they block projects that forget them.
Who you need on your side

items: **Sponsor:** owns the budget and the metric. Give them a short written update every week.
**Champion:** a respected user who wants this to work. Build for them first.
**IT and security:** involve them in week one. Ask what they need from you before they ask.
**Sceptic:** the person whose spreadsheet you are replacing. Their objections are your test cases.

blocks.text: Saying no without losing the room

Never a bare no. Say what it would cost, what it would delay, and offer a smaller version: "I can add that. It pushes go-live by two weeks. A filter on the existing view gets most of it by Friday. Which do you prefer?"
Delivering bad news
Early, in person or by call, with the cause, the impact, and what you have already done. Follow in writing the same day.
Section 7 · end to end

This is the bakery story at company size. Bread becomes chilled food on trucks. The head baker becomes a dispatcher. The bake slip becomes an alert screen. Wasted loaves become temperature write-offs. Follow the same five steps.

Kestrel Cold Chain is an invented company, and every figure below is made up for training. It distributes chilled and frozen food from 14 warehouses to supermarkets. Your company sold them a data platform. You are the lead FDE, with one other engineer, and you have twelve weeks.
The brief from the first meeting, in the COO's words: *"We are losing too much product and too many deliveries are late. We bought your platform. We want AI to fix it."*
Weeks 1 to 2 · Discover
The brief contains two problems, no metric and a solution nobody has defined. You do not start building. You spend the first week in a warehouse and in the dispatch office.
Site log, week 1

rows: Finance: product written off for temperature breach was 3.1% of shipped value last quarter. This is the number the board sees.
Night shift, Leeds site. Truck sensors record temperature every 5 minutes, but the file is only downloaded when the truck returns. Nobody sees a breach while it is happening.
Dispatcher Meera keeps her own spreadsheet of "trucks I worry about". She phones drivers when a route runs long on a hot day. Her instinct is the prototype.
IT: the warehouse system is SQL Server on-premise. The transport system is SaaS with a REST API, 600 calls per hour. Sensor vendor can push files to SFTP every 15 minutes if asked.
Site IDs do not match between warehouse and transport systems. 14 sites, 3 naming schemes.
CISO: no client data may leave their cloud account. The platform is already deployed in their VPC. Service accounts need a two-week review.

blocks.text: Candidates ranked with the ops head. A is chosen. Positions are the team's estimates.

items: **A. Live breach-risk alerts for trucks in transit.** High impact, data mostly exists, one clear user.
**B. Full route optimisation.** High impact, months of work, replaces a system they just bought.
**C. Demand forecasting.** Useful, needs retailer data they do not have yet.
**D. Daily write-off report.** Easy, but it only describes losses after the fact.
**E. Chatbot over all company documents.** What "AI" meant to one executive. No owner, no metric.

blocks.text: End of week 2 · Scope
Scope statement, signed by the COO

items: **User:** the six dispatchers on shift.
**Decision:** which trucks to call, reroute or swap in the next four hours.
**Metric:** temperature write-offs as a share of shipped value. Baseline 3.1%. Target 2.0% within one quarter of rollout.
**Data:** shipments (warehouse system), routes and ETAs (transport API), sensor readings (SFTP), outside temperature (public weather feed).
**Out of scope:** route optimisation, forecasting, any change to the transport system. Late deliveries are tracked but not targeted.

blocks.text: Notice what happened to "AI". You did not argue about it. You tied the engagement to a number the board already watches, and left room for a model once rules have proved the workflow.
Weeks 3 to 5 · Prototype

The goal is to learn whether dispatchers act on an alert, not to build the final system. So you take every shortcut that does not put client data at risk: a nightly extract instead of CDC, a read replica, rules instead of a model, two warehouses instead of fourteen.
Python 3.10+. Run with five sample trucks; each returned the expected level. Example: 3.0 C rising 0.5 C per hour, 6 h from arrival, gives AT_RISK.

Every alert carries its reason in plain words. Dispatchers will not act on a score they cannot check. The `UNKNOWN` level matters as much as the others: a silent sensor must never look like a safe truck.

In week 4 Meera and two colleagues use the screen next to their old spreadsheet. You sit behind them. Three findings change the design: they want trucks sorted by time left, they need the driver's phone number on the row, and a third of alerts are false because door-open events at delivery stops look like warming. You add a rule that ignores readings within ten minutes of a stop.
At the end of week 5 Meera stops updating her spreadsheet. That is the gate.
Weeks 6 to 10 · Productionise
Same logic, different guarantees. Production replaces every manual step with a scheduled one, adds identity and permissions in front, and adds monitoring so a failure reaches a named person.

rows: Shipments loaded this morning must appear within minutes
Vendor pushes to SFTP every 15 minutes, with a freshness alert
The alert window is four hours, so stale data is a silent failure
Crosswalk table for 14 sites, owned by the ops analyst
New depots must not need an engineer
Versioned service with tests and stored alert history
You need to explain any past alert and compare rule versions
SSO, dispatchers see only their region
It has to survive you leaving

blocks.code:
# Contract for the sensor feed, agreed with the telematics vendor.
dataset: sensor_readings
owner: telematics vendor helpdesk
escalation: Kestrel fleet manager
delivery: SFTP, one file per 15 minutes, name readings_YYYYMMDD_HHMM.csv
freshness_sla: newest reading no older than 30 minutes
columns:
  - {name: truck_id,    type: string,    required: true}
  - {name: read_at_utc, type: timestamp, required: true}
  - {name: temp_c,      type: decimal,   required: true, min: -40, max: 40}
  - {name: door_open,   type: boolean,   required: false}
checks:
  - unique: [truck_id, read_at_utc]
  - on_breaking_change: reject file, alert both sides

blocks.text: An illustrative data contract. It parses as valid YAML. The field names are this manual's, not a specific tool's format.

Two things nearly sink the timeline. The service account review takes three weeks, not two. You had asked in week 1, so it lands in week 6 and not week 9. Then in week 8 a transport system upgrade renames a field and ETAs go null for a morning. The quality check catches it, the app shows "ETA unavailable" instead of wrong risk levels, and you add a contract with that team too.
Rollout goes two sites, then six, then all fourteen. Each wave starts with you on site for the first shift.
Weeks 11 to 12 · Hand over and expand
Invented result for the scenario. The rate crosses the 2.0% target in week 8 when all sites are live. In a real engagement you would also check the same weeks last year, since heat is seasonal.
Handover checklist

items: Kestrel's data engineer fixes a staged pipeline failure alone, using the runbook.
The ops analyst adds a new depot to the crosswalk without help.
Alert thresholds are editable by the ops head, with history.
The COO's weekly report pulls the metric from the platform.
Support path written down: client on-call first, then vendor support, then you.

blocks.text: Field report to product

items: SFTP connector needs a built-in freshness alert. We wrote one by hand.
No way to show "data unavailable" per field in the app builder. We worked around it.
The door-open filter is likely useful to every cold-chain client. Proposing it as a template.
Next use case agreed with the COO: a model to replace the slope rule, trained on eight weeks of labelled alerts.

blocks.text: The last bullet is where "AI" returns, now with data, a user and a baseline to beat. That is the normal order: fix the workflow with something simple, then let a model improve a step that is already measured.

blocks.title: Debrief: what were the three decisions that mattered most?
blocks.text: One, refusing to build before the metric was agreed. Two, asking security for access in week 1 so the slow review ran in parallel. Three, shipping rules with reasons before any model, which earned dispatcher trust and produced the labelled data a model needs.

blocks.title: Debrief: what would you do differently?
blocks.text: Get a contract with the transport system team before production, not after their upgrade broke the feed. Also capture a comparison group of routes without alerts for a few weeks, so the improvement can be separated from weather.
Come back to this section after you are comfortable with 1 to 7. It covers what changes when you lead a team, run a whole customer account, or deploy AI agents.
Deploying AI agents at a client

items: Start from one workflow step with a clear input and output, not from "an assistant".
Build an evaluation set from real client cases before tuning anything. Fifty labelled examples beat opinions.
Ground answers in the client's data through retrieval or tools, and show the source.
Respect permissions: the model may only see what the asking user may see.
Put a human approval step on any action that changes a system of record.
Track cost per task and latency along with accuracy, and log every run.

blocks.text: Build once, generalise after

items: First client: solve it by hand and note every workaround.
Second client with the same need: extract a template.
Third: push it into the product with the product team.
Keep client-specific logic in configuration, away from core code.
Write gap reports with evidence: who hit it, how often, what it cost.

blocks.text: Running an account as lead

items: Keep a one-page account plan: sponsor goals, use cases live, next two, risks.
Protect your team's focus. One goal per week, said out loud.
Hold a regular executive review that shows the metric, not the activity.
Plan for the champion leaving. Have a second one.
Know the commercial side: renewal date, what expansion depends on.

blocks.text: Technical judgement under pressure

items: Decide what is throwaway and say so. Prototype code that quietly becomes production is the common failure.
Prefer boring technology the client's team can run.
Design the rollback before the rollout.
When estimates are uncertain, give a range and the fact that would narrow it.
Never trade away security or data correctness for a date.

rows: Impressive prototype, nobody uses it after week six
Build with a named user from day one, measure usage
Signed scope, a visible "next" list, trade-offs stated each time
Only the FDE can fix it
Runbook, staged failure drill, client on-call before you leave
Heavy custom code that blocks upgrades
Configuration over forks, upstream the gaps
Go-live blocked by a review nobody started
Meet security in week one with your data flow diagram
Team celebrates features, sponsor sees no change
One metric, on a dashboard, in every update

blocks.text: One story is not enough to see the pattern. Here are six short ones from different industries. Each has the same five parts as the bakery: what the client said, what was really wrong, the data, what was built, and the number that moved. All six are invented composites of common engagement types.
Hospital: beds stay full after patients are ready to leave

rows: Patients cleared by the doctor wait hours for pharmacy, transport or paperwork. Nobody sees which step is stuck.
Admission system, pharmacy orders, porter requests on paper.
A ward screen listing each ready patient with the one task blocking them and its owner.
Hours from "medically ready" to discharge: 6.5 to 3.
The request named a solution. Discovery found the problem.

blocks.text: Bank: analysts drown in fraud alerts

rows: The existing rules already catch fraud. Analysts spend 20 minutes per alert collecting facts from five screens.
Transactions, customer profile, device history, past case notes.
One case page with all facts joined, plus an AI-written summary that cites each source and that the analyst approves.
Minutes per alert: 20 to 7. Decisions stay with humans.
In regulated work, speed up the human. Do not replace the decision.

blocks.text: Factory: machines stop without warning

rows: Sensor data exists but sits on each machine. Maintenance logs are handwritten, so there are no failure labels.
Vibration and temperature sensors, shift logbooks, spare-part orders.
First a digital logbook and simple threshold alerts. A model came six months later, once labels existed.
Unplanned stops per month on one line: 11 to 6.
No labelled history means no model yet. Build the data first.

blocks.text: Retailer: shelves empty while the warehouse is full

rows: Zero sales were read as zero demand, so out-of-stock items were ordered less and less.
Till sales, stock snapshots, deliveries, product master with duplicate codes.
A daily "will run out before next delivery" list per store, with stock-outs flagged apart from true low demand.
On-shelf availability of the top 500 items: 91% to 96%.
Question what a zero in the data means before trusting it.

blocks.text: Insurer: claims take three weeks

rows: Two of the three weeks are spent waiting for a missing document that nobody asked for on day one.
Claim forms as PDFs, policy system, email threads.
Document extraction that checks completeness at submission and tells the customer at once what is missing.
Median days to settle a simple claim: 21 to 8.
Measure where the time goes before choosing what to automate.

blocks.text: Software company: support cannot keep up

rows: 40% of tickets are five known questions. The answers are in outdated help pages.
Two years of tickets, help centre, product changelog.
Help pages fixed first. Then a retrieval assistant that drafts replies with citations, tested on 200 past tickets before launch.
Tickets solved without a human: 0% to 28%, with wrong answers under 2% on the test set.
An AI assistant is only as good as the documents behind it. Build the test set first.

blocks.title: Check yourself: what do all six have in common with the bakery?
blocks.text: The client asked for a solution, and the FDE went looking for the problem. In each case the real cause was found by watching the work and measuring it, the first build was simpler than what was asked for, and success was one number the client already cared about.
Section 11 · learn by building

Reading does not get you hired. A project you can demo does. Paid FDE courses are built around guided projects and a final capstone shown to a panel. These four follow the same ladder and cost nothing but time. Do them in order. Each one ends with something you can show.
Each project keeps everything from the one before and adds one new skill. The capstone is amber because its hard part is the client side, not the code.
Level: beginner · Time: one weekend · Tools: SQL, a spreadsheet or Python
Rebuild the Start here example yourself.

items: Invent 8 weeks of data in two CSV files: sales (shop, date, loaves sold) and baking (shop name, date, loaves baked). Use different shop names in the two files on purpose.
Load both into a database. Write the lookup that matches the shop names.
Write one query: for each shop and weekday, average sold over the last four weeks.
Produce tomorrow's bake list. Compare waste under your list with waste under "same every day".
Write a five-line scope statement and a half-page result note for the owner.

blocks.text: **Proves:** you can go from a vague complaint to a metric and a working answer.
Level: basic to intermediate · Time: one week · Tools: Python, PostgreSQL, a scheduler
Invented client: a city transport office asking why some routes are always late.

items: Pick one public API and one downloadable file on the same subject, for example trips and weather.
Build raw, clean and model layers. Keep the raw copy untouched.
Make the load incremental and safe to run twice.
Add five quality checks: freshness, row count, unique key, nulls, valid range.
Schedule it daily and make it message you when it fails. Break it on purpose once and fix it from your own runbook.

blocks.text: **Proves:** the data integration skills in section 4, which interviews test hardest.
Level: intermediate · Time: two weeks · Tools: Python, an LLM API, a vector store
Invented client: a company whose staff keep asking HR the same policy questions.

items: Collect 20 to 30 public documents, for example a university's or a government office's policies.
Write 40 real questions with correct answers and the source page. This is your test set. Do it before any code.
Build retrieval plus answer, and make every answer show its source.
Let it say "I do not know" when the documents do not cover the question.
Score it on the test set. Change one thing at a time and re-score. Record cost and response time per question.

blocks.text: **Proves:** you can deploy AI the way section 8 describes: measured, grounded, honest about limits.

lessons.title: 4. Capstone: a real person as your client

blocks.text: Level: advanced · Time: three to four weeks · Tools: your choice
Find a real small business or team: a shop, a clinic, a college club, a relative's office. This is the full job.

items: **Week 1, discover.** Watch them work for two sessions. Keep a site log. Rank three problems by value and effort.
**Week 1, scope.** Agree one metric with a baseline and a target. Get a yes in writing, even by message.
**Week 2, prototype.** Something rough they use for real within seven days.
**Week 3, harden.** Automate the manual steps, add checks and a failure alert, write a one-page runbook.
**Week 4, hand over.** They run it without you for a week. Measure the metric again.
**Demo.** Record ten minutes: problem, metric, what you built, result, what you would do next.

blocks.text: **Proves:** everything. This is the story you tell in every interview round.
What a finished project folder contains

Shows you define the problem before coding

One picture from sources to user
You can explain a system in a minute

Others can pick up your work

blocks.text: Section 9 gives you questions and answers. This section shows how the interview days usually run, gives a way to structure any answer, and walks through one full mock case so you can hear what a good answer sounds like.

A common shape for the loop. Order and number of rounds differ by company, and AI companies often add a round on building with models. The grey line under each box says where this manual prepares you for it.
For any vague case: C-U-M-D-B-R

items: **Clarify:** ask what "bad" means and what it costs.
**User:** name who does the work and who decides.
**Metric:** propose one number with a baseline.
**Data:** list sources and what might be wrong with each.
**Build:** the smallest first version, in one week.
**Risks:** access, adoption, privacy, and what you would check first.

blocks.text: For any behavioural question: STAR, plus a lesson

items: **Situation:** two sentences of context.
**Task:** what you were responsible for.
**Action:** what you did. Say "I", not "we".
**Result:** a number if you have one.
**Lesson:** what you do differently now.
Keep it under two minutes. Stop, and let them ask.

blocks.text: Read it once. Then cover the "You" lines and try answering each interviewer line aloud before looking.

rows: A food delivery company says its customer refunds are too high. You start Monday. What do you do?
First I would like to understand the size and shape of it. What share of orders gets refunded today, and has it changed recently? And who told us it is too high: finance, or operations?
About 4% of orders, up from 2.5% a year ago. Finance raised it.

So the metric is refund rate, baseline 4%, and a sensible first target is back toward 2.5%. Before proposing anything I would spend the first days with the support agents who approve refunds, and pull refund reasons from the data. My guess is there are a few very different causes hiding in one number: late delivery, missing items, wrong items, and abuse.

Orders, refunds with reason codes, delivery timestamps, restaurant and rider IDs, and support chat logs. I would check early whether the reason codes are reliable, because agents often pick the first option. If they are not, I would read a sample of 100 chats by hand to get a true split.
Say missing items from a small set of restaurants are 40% of refunds.

Then my first build is small: a weekly list of restaurants ranked by missing-item refunds per 100 orders, sent to the partner team with the specific items. No model. I would pilot it in one city for two weeks and measure refund rate there against a similar city without it.
The VP wants an AI that auto-approves refunds instead.

I would ask what outcome they want from that. If it is agent time, auto-approval may help and I can scope it as a second phase with limits and human review above an amount. But it would not lower the refund rate, and could raise it. I would show both options with their effect on the number finance cares about and let them choose.

Three things. Data access may take weeks, so I would request it on day one. The partner team may not act on the list, so I need their manager involved from the start. And refund rate is seasonal, which is why I want a comparison city and not only before and after.
Starts proposing a solution at once
Asks for size, trend and who cares, then restates the problem
Says the plan in order, then follows it
Names sources and doubts one of them for a stated reason
Proposes a large platform or a model first
Agrees with the VP or dismisses the VP
Finds the goal behind the request, offers options with trade-offs
Access, adoption and measurement named without being asked

These descriptions come from the providers' own pages. I have not taken the courses and cannot vouch for quality or price. Check recent independent reviews, the refund policy and the instructor's field experience before paying.

questions.q: In an AI-assisted pair coding round, how do you work?
questions.a: Say the plan first, then use the assistant for boilerplate while I keep control of the design. I read every line it produces, run it, and write a test for the risky part. Interviewers watch whether I can direct the tool and catch its mistakes, not whether I type fast.

questions.q: Tell me about a project you built end to end.
questions.a: Use your capstone. Start with the client and the problem in one sentence, then the metric and baseline, what you built first, what changed after users tried it, the result as a number, and what you would do next. Keep code details for follow-up questions.

questions.q: The client asks for a specific solution, such as a chatbot. How do you respond?
questions.a: I treat the request as a clue, not a requirement. I ask what they hope it will change and how they would know. Often a simpler step delivers that result faster. I then offer both options with their effect on the metric and let the client choose.

questions.q: What do you prepare for a client's procurement or security review?
questions.a: A data flow diagram showing what data moves where, a list of access needed with least privilege, where data is stored and for how long, how users log in, how actions are logged, and the incident process. Bringing this to the first meeting saves weeks.

questions.q: How do I show FDE skills if I have never had the title?
questions.a: Do one project with a real person as the client and keep the evidence: scope statement, site log, working tool, result note and a short demo. Then describe your past work the same way: who asked, what was unclear, what you shipped, what number moved.

questions.q: What is an FDE in one sentence?
questions.a: A software engineer who works at the customer, finds their real problem, and builds on top of the company's product until that problem is solved and the customer can run the solution alone.

questions.q: What does forward deployed mean?
questions.a: The phrase comes from the military, where it describes units placed close to the action. Here it means an engineer placed close to the customer, often in their office, and not back at headquarters with the product team.

questions.q: How would you explain the job to a shopkeeper?
questions.a: A factory makes one shirt for everyone. I am the tailor who visits one customer, measures, and alters the shirt until it fits. Then I tell the factory which sizes people keep asking for.

questions.q: Who is the client, and which people at the client matter?
questions.a: The client is the company that bought the product. Three groups matter: the sponsor who pays and owns the result, the users who will work with what you build, and IT and security who control access to systems and data.

questions.q: What is the difference between a prototype and production?
questions.a: A prototype is a quick version built to learn whether the idea works, often with manual steps. Production runs every day without you, is tested and monitored, and someone at the client owns it. At the bakery, the hand-filled sheet was the prototype and the nightly printed slip was production.

questions.q: What do POC, pilot and production mean?
questions.a: A proof of concept shows the idea is possible, usually on sample data. A pilot is real use by a small group, such as two sites. Production is everyone using it as the normal way of working.

questions.q: What is an API, in plain words?
questions.a: A counter where one program asks another for data or asks it to do something, in an agreed format. A weather app asks a weather service through its API. FDEs use APIs to pull data out of the client's tools.

questions.q: What is a data pipeline?
questions.a: A set of steps that copies data from where it is created to where it is needed, cleaning it on the way, on a schedule. At the bakery: read sales from billing each night, join with the baking notebook, write tomorrow's bake list.

questions.q: What are a metric, a baseline and a target?
questions.a: The metric is the number you agree to improve. The baseline is its value today. The target is the value you aim for. Bakery: loaves wasted per day, baseline 60, target 20. Without these three, nobody can say whether the project worked.

questions.q: Do I need a computer science degree?
questions.a: There is no single rule and it varies by company. Interviews test what you can do: write working code, handle data with SQL, design a simple system, and talk through an unclear problem. A portfolio project that shows all four counts for a lot.

questions.q: Can a mobile or frontend developer become an FDE?
questions.a: Yes. You already build for real users and ship to production, which is the heart of the role. The usual gaps are SQL, data pipelines and cloud basics. Close those, and practise describing your past work in terms of who asked and what improved.

questions.q: Which languages and tools should I learn first?
questions.a: SQL and Python first, because almost every engagement needs them. Then git, calling REST APIs, Docker, and the basics of one cloud. TypeScript helps when you build user-facing apps.

questions.q: How much of the job is coding and how much is meetings?
questions.a: It changes by phase. Early on it is mostly listening and looking at data. In the middle it is mostly building. Near the end there is more testing, documentation and teaching. Across a whole engagement, expect to code on most days.

questions.q: Is there a lot of travel?
questions.a: It depends on the company and the client. Some roles are several days a week at the client, some are mostly remote with visits. Ask about it directly in the interview, because it shapes daily life in this job.

questions.q: What other names does this role have?
questions.a: Forward Deployed Software Engineer, deployed engineer, customer engineer, and at Palantir the nickname Delta. Solutions engineer and implementation engineer overlap with it at some companies. Read the job description for how much production coding is expected.

questions.q: I am totally new. What should I do in my first month?
questions.a: Weeks one and two: SQL every day. Week three: a small Python script that pulls data from a public API into a database. Week four: pick an invented client, write a five-line scope, and build a tiny tool on that data. That is the whole job in miniature.

questions.q: Walk me through how you would run a project end to end.
questions.a: Discover: watch the work and rank problems by value. Scope: one user, one decision, one metric, signed by the sponsor. Prototype: a quick version on real data with a real user. Productionise: automate, test, secure and monitor it. Hand over: the client runs it alone, and I report gaps to product and agree the next use case.

questions.q: What do you ask in a first client meeting?
questions.a: What is going wrong and what it costs. Who feels it day to day. How they handle it today. What they tried before. What number would show it is fixed. Then I ask to watch someone do the work, because what people do differs from what they describe.

questions.q: What is a primary key and why does it matter for integration?
questions.a: A column, or set of columns, that identifies each row uniquely. It lets you update the right row instead of adding duplicates, and it is what you join on. Much integration pain comes from sources with no reliable key.

questions.q: What is the difference between a database, a data warehouse and a data lake?
questions.a: A database runs an application and handles many small reads and writes. A data warehouse stores cleaned data from many systems for analysis. A data lake stores raw files of any kind cheaply, to be shaped later.

questions.q: What is the difference between cloud and on-premise?
questions.a: Cloud means the software runs on computers rented from a provider and reached over the internet. On-premise means it runs on machines in the client's own building or data centre. Clients choose on-premise for control, regulation or secrecy, and it makes deployment and support slower.

questions.q: What is API pagination and how do you handle it?
questions.a: An API returns large results in pages. You request a page, read the marker for the next one, and repeat until there is none. Handle rate limits between calls, save progress so a failure can resume, and deduplicate by ID in case a record moves between pages.

questions.q: What do you put in a weekly status update?
questions.a: Four short parts: what was done, what was learned, what is blocked and who can unblock it, and what happens next week. Put the metric at the top. Keep it short enough to read on a phone.

questions.q: What is retrieval-augmented generation, in plain words?
questions.a: Before the model answers, the system looks up relevant passages from the client's own documents or data and gives them to the model with the question. The answer is then based on that material and can cite it, instead of relying on what the model happened to learn in training.

questions.q: What does a Forward Deployed Engineer do?
questions.a: An FDE is a software engineer embedded with a customer. They find the customer's most valuable problem, connect the customer's data to the company's product, build what is missing, and stay until it runs in production and people use it. They also report field gaps back to the product team.

questions.q: How is an FDE different from a product software engineer?
questions.a: A product engineer builds general features for all customers and rarely meets users. An FDE builds specific solutions for one customer, works with their people daily, and is measured on that customer's outcome. The FDE trades depth in one codebase for breadth across data, infrastructure and communication.

questions.q: How is an FDE different from a solutions engineer or a consultant?
questions.a: A solutions engineer mainly supports the sale with demos and proofs of concept. A consultant often delivers advice or configuration. An FDE writes production code after the sale and owns the result. The line varies by company, so ask how much time the role spends coding.

questions.q: Why do you want to be an FDE and not a regular engineer?
questions.a: A strong answer names what you get from the role: seeing the direct effect of your work, variety of problems, and learning a business quickly. Back it with an example where you worked closely with users. Avoid saying you want less coding, because the role codes a lot.

questions.q: How do you measure success in an engagement?
questions.a: By a business metric agreed with the sponsor at the start, with a baseline and a target. Secondary signals are adoption (do people use it daily), whether the client can run it without me, and whether the account grows to a second use case.

questions.q: What is the hardest part of the job?
questions.a: Holding two contexts at once. You must go deep enough technically to ship correct software, and stay close enough to the client to know whether it is the right software. Travel, changing priorities and being the face of every problem are also real costs.

questions.q: When should custom client work become a product feature?
questions.a: When a second or third client needs the same thing, or when the workaround is costly to maintain. I write up the gap with evidence, build the client version so it can be extracted, and work with product on the general design. One request from one client is usually configuration, not roadmap.

questions.q: A client wants heavy customisation that will block future upgrades. What do you do?
questions.a: I find the need behind the request, then look for a way to meet it through configuration or an extension point. If a fork is the only route, I explain the upgrade cost to the client in plain terms and raise it with product. I do not silently build a snowflake, because both sides pay for it later.

questions.q: A client says: we want AI to fix our operations. What is your first step?
questions.a: I do not propose a solution. I ask what is going wrong, what it costs, and who feels it. Then I watch the workflow in person. The goal of the first week is a ranked list of concrete problems with a number attached to each.

questions.q: What does a good scope statement contain?
questions.a: The user, the decision being improved, one metric with baseline and target, the data sources with their owners, and an explicit out-of-scope list. If it does not fit on half a page, it is not scoped yet.

questions.q: How do you choose between several candidate problems?
questions.a: I place them on impact against effort with the client, and check three things for the top option: a named user who wants it, data that already exists, and a metric the sponsor reports. I prefer a smaller problem I can prove in weeks over a bigger one that takes a quarter.

questions.q: The client cannot tell you what success looks like. How do you proceed?
questions.a: I ask what they report upward and what gets them a difficult call from their boss. I propose a metric myself and let them correct it. If there is truly no measurable outcome, I say so, and suggest a short discovery phase with a go or no-go at the end.

questions.q: How do you handle scope creep mid-project?
questions.a: I keep a visible list of requests. For each new one I state the cost and what it would displace, then let the sponsor choose. Most requests move to the next phase once the trade-off is clear. The signed scope makes this a planning conversation and not a refusal.

questions.q: Case: a hospital group says patient discharge is too slow. Scope it.
questions.a: I would clarify what slow means and where time is lost: waiting for tests, pharmacy, transport, paperwork or a bed elsewhere. I would shadow discharge coordinators and get timestamps for each step. A likely first scope is a live list of patients medically ready with the blocking task and owner, measured by hours from ready to discharged. I would flag patient data rules and involve clinical leadership and security from the start.

questions.q: Case: a retailer wants to reduce stock-outs. What data do you ask for and what do you build first?
questions.a: Sales by product, store and day, inventory snapshots, deliveries, and the product and store master data. I would first check whether stock-outs are even recorded, since zero sales can mean no stock or no demand. A first build is a daily list of products likely to run out in each store before the next delivery, using simple rate-of-sale rules, checked against store managers' judgement.

questions.q: How do you estimate when half the facts are unknown?
questions.a: I give a range, name the two or three unknowns that drive it, and say what would narrow it. For example: four to eight weeks, depending on database access and on how clean the site IDs are. I will know after the first week of data profiling. Then I update the estimate when I learn more.

questions.q: Explain ETL versus ELT.
questions.a: ETL transforms data before loading it into the target. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse. ELT is the common choice now because storage is cheap and keeping raw data lets you redo transformations without re-extracting.

questions.q: What is an idempotent pipeline and why does it matter?
questions.a: Running it twice with the same input gives the same result as running it once. It matters because pipelines fail and get retried. You achieve it with stable keys and upserts or by replacing whole partitions, never by blind appends.

questions.q: How do you find and remove duplicate rows in SQL?
questions.a: Use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the business key and ordered by a recency column, then keep row number 1. Before deleting, I check why duplicates exist, since they may be real distinct events with a missing key column.

questions.q: What is change data capture?
questions.a: CDC reads the database transaction log and emits inserts, updates and deletes as they occur. It gives near real-time data with low load on the source and captures deletes, which timestamp-based polling misses. It needs log access and careful handling of schema changes.

questions.q: How would you load data incrementally from a REST API with rate limits?
questions.a: Use an updated-since parameter or cursor and store the high-water mark after each successful run. Page through results, back off on 429 responses, and overlap the window slightly to catch late updates, deduplicating on the record ID. Schedule a periodic full reconcile to catch deletes.

questions.q: Two systems have no shared customer ID. How do you join them?
questions.a: Entity resolution. Normalise names, emails, phones and addresses. Match on exact strong identifiers first, then fuzzy matching within blocks such as the same postcode. Send uncertain pairs to a human reviewer and store the result in a crosswalk table that both sides can audit.

questions.q: What data quality checks do you put on every pipeline?
questions.a: Freshness, row count compared with recent runs, uniqueness and non-null on keys, referential integrity to parent tables, and valid ranges on important fields. Critical failures stop the pipeline. Warnings go to a channel someone reads.

questions.q: Write a query for the latest status of each shipment.
questions.a: SELECT * FROM (SELECT s.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shipment_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM shipment_status s) t WHERE rn = 1. I would mention a tiebreaker column in the ORDER BY if timestamps can collide.

questions.q: How do you handle schema changes in a source you do not control?
questions.a: Detect them at ingest by comparing against the expected schema. Additive changes pass through with a notice. Removed or retyped columns fail the load loudly. Then I set up a data contract with the owner so changes are announced first.

questions.q: What is a slowly changing dimension and when do you need type 2?
questions.a: It is reference data that changes over time, such as a customer's region. Type 1 overwrites the old value. Type 2 keeps history with valid-from and valid-to dates. You need type 2 when past facts must be reported against the value that was true at the time.

questions.q: A dashboard number does not match the client's finance report. How do you investigate?
questions.a: I get the exact definition and filters of the finance number first. Then I reconcile at a small grain, such as one day and one site, and compare row by row. Usual causes are different time zones or cut-off times, excluded categories, currency handling, duplicates from a join, or late-arriving records.

questions.q: What is an ontology or semantic layer and why do FDEs care?
questions.a: It is a model of business objects, their properties, links and actions, on top of raw tables. Users and applications work with shipments and customers and not with joins. It gives consistent definitions, a place to attach permissions, and a clean interface for apps and AI agents.

questions.q: When is streaming the right choice over batch?
questions.a: When the decision has to be made within seconds or minutes of the event, such as fraud checks or live equipment alerts. For anything decided hourly or daily, batch or micro-batch is cheaper, easier to test and easier to backfill.

questions.q: Design an integration that pulls orders from a client's on-premise database into your cloud platform.
questions.a: Clarify volume, freshness need and network rules. A common design is an agent inside the client network that reads through CDC or incremental queries with a read-only account, and pushes outbound over TLS so no inbound firewall port is opened. Land raw data, then transform. Add checkpointing, retries, monitoring and a backfill path.

questions.q: How do you make a pipeline safe to retry and backfill?
questions.a: Deterministic inputs per run, such as a date partition. Writes that replace or upsert by key. No side effects inside transforms. A parameter to run any historical window. Then retries and backfills are the same operation as a normal run.

questions.q: How would you add SSO to a client-facing application?
questions.a: Integrate with their identity provider using OIDC or SAML. Map IdP groups to application roles so access is managed where the client already manages it. Support automatic user provisioning if offered. Test logout, session expiry and the case of a user removed from a group.

questions.q: What changes when you deploy into the client's own cloud account?
questions.a: They own the network, identity and often the release approval. You need infrastructure as code they can review, least-privilege roles, private connectivity, and a way to get logs and metrics that fits their rules. Upgrades need a schedule agreed with them.

questions.q: How do you ship and support software in an air-gapped environment?
questions.a: Package everything, including images and dependencies, into a signed versioned bundle that installs offline. Test it in a replica with no internet. Include built-in health checks and a diagnostics export the client can hand to you. Releases are less frequent, so each one needs a tested rollback.

questions.q: Design an alerting system for at-risk deliveries.
questions.a: Inputs are positions, ETAs, sensor data and delivery windows. A scheduled or streaming job computes risk per delivery, stores every evaluation, and raises an alert only on state change to avoid noise. The alert shows the reason and a suggested action. I would add suppression rules, an acknowledgement flow, and measure precision with user feedback.

questions.q: How do you design row-level permissions for a multi-region client?
questions.a: Attach a region attribute to each object and a region entitlement to each user or group from the identity provider. Enforce the filter in the data layer and not in the user interface, so every app and API inherits it. Test with real personas and log access.

questions.q: How do you take a prototype to production without a rewrite?
questions.a: I decide early which parts are throwaway and which are the core. Core logic is written as tested functions from day one, even if the plumbing around it is manual. Productionising then replaces the plumbing: scheduling, ingestion, auth and monitoring. If the prototype was pure exploration, I say so and budget a rebuild.

questions.q: What do you monitor on a production data product?
questions.a: Pipeline success and duration, data freshness per source, quality check results, application errors and latency, and usage by real users. Above all the outcome metric. Each alert has an owner and a runbook entry.

questions.q: What coding questions should I expect?
questions.a: Practical ones more often than puzzle-style ones: parse a messy file, merge records, group and aggregate, call a paginated API, implement a small rate limiter or cache. Expect follow-ups about edge cases, tests and what you would change for production.

questions.q: Parse a log file and return the top five error messages by count. How do you approach it?
questions.a: Read line by line so large files do not exhaust memory, extract the level and message with a clear rule or regular expression, count with a dictionary or Counter, and return the five most common. I would state assumptions about the format and handle malformed lines without crashing.

questions.q: Merge two lists of customer records with different field names. What matters?
questions.a: A clear mapping to one schema, normalising values such as case and whitespace, choosing the match key, and a rule for conflicts, such as most recently updated wins. I would keep the source of each field for audit and write tests for conflicts and missing keys.

questions.q: Implement retry with exponential backoff. What are the details?
questions.a: Retry only on transient errors such as timeouts, 429 and 5xx. Double the wait each attempt up to a cap, add random jitter so clients do not retry in step, and stop after a maximum number of attempts. The operation must be idempotent or carry an idempotency key.

questions.q: How do you process a file too large for memory?
questions.a: Stream it in chunks, keep only running aggregates or write partial results to disk, and use a database or an external sort if a full sort or join is needed. In Python that means iterating the file or using chunked readers.

questions.q: How do you test data transformation code?
questions.a: Unit tests with small hand-made inputs that cover nulls, duplicates, bad types and boundary values. A snapshot test on a realistic sample. Data checks that run in production on every load. Pure functions for the logic make all of this easy.

questions.q: You inherit an undocumented client script that feeds a critical report. How do you change it safely?
questions.a: Capture its current output on real inputs as a baseline first. Read it and add characterisation tests. Make the smallest change, compare the output with the baseline, and explain every difference. Deploy next to the old version for a period before switching.

questions.q: How do you balance speed and code quality on site?
questions.a: I decide per component. Exploration code is quick and labelled as throwaway. Anything that will carry production data gets tests, review and clear names from the start. I never cut corners on correctness of client data or on security.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you explained something technical to a non-technical person.
questions.a: Use situation, action, result. Good answers show you started from what the listener cared about, used their vocabulary and one concrete example, checked understanding, and that a decision followed.

questions.q: How do you build trust with a new client team?
questions.a: Listen first and learn their work. Deliver something small and useful quickly. Do exactly what I said I would do, write clear updates, and admit mistakes early. Respect their systems and rules, especially IT and security.

questions.q: A senior stakeholder insists on a solution you think is wrong. What do you do?
questions.a: I ask what outcome they want from it, then show evidence, ideally a quick test on their data, for the option I recommend. I present trade-offs and let them decide. If they still choose their way and it is not harmful, I commit to it and set a checkpoint to review results.

questions.q: You will miss a deadline you committed to. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Tell the client as soon as I know, not on the due date. Explain the cause, the new date, what I have done to reduce the delay, and offer options such as a reduced first delivery. Then meet the new date.

questions.q: Users are not adopting what you built. What now?
questions.a: Sit with them and watch. Usually it does not fit a step of their real workflow, they do not trust the data, or the old tool is still required by their manager. I fix the specific friction, show them a case where it was right, and ask their manager to make it the standard way of working.

questions.q: The client's IT team is slow and blocking you. What do you do?
questions.a: Meet them in person, learn their process and constraints, and give them exactly what they need in their format. Start requests early and run other work in parallel. If it still threatens the timeline, I raise it with the sponsor as a shared risk, without blaming IT.

questions.q: How do you say no to a client?
questions.a: With a reason and an alternative. I state what the request would cost or delay, offer a smaller version or a later phase, and ask them to choose. That keeps the decision with them and the relationship intact.

questions.q: Your pipeline pushed wrong numbers into an executive report. Walk me through your response.
questions.a: Stop the harm first: pause the pipeline or roll back, and mark the report as under review. Tell the sponsor immediately with what is known. Find the cause, correct the data, and confirm the fix with the report owner. Then send a short written review with the cause and the new check that prevents a repeat.

questions.q: Two client departments want opposite things from your project. How do you resolve it?
questions.a: I make the conflict explicit, with each side's goal and the cost of each option, and bring it to the sponsor who owns the outcome. I look for a design that serves the shared metric. I do not pick a winner myself, and I do not build both quietly.

questions.q: Your champion at the client leaves the company. What do you do?
questions.a: I should already have a second supporter. I meet the replacement quickly, show the results in their terms, and ask what they need. I also check that knowledge and ownership of the solution are documented and not held by the person who left.

questions.q: How do you work with your own sales and product teams?
questions.a: With sales, I give honest views on what is feasible and by when, and flag expansion chances I see on site. With product, I send evidence-based gap reports and help design the general solution. I do not promise the client roadmap items I do not control.

questions.q: A client wants an LLM assistant over their internal documents. How do you approach it?
questions.a: Pick one user group and the questions they ask most. Build an evaluation set of real questions with correct answers. Use retrieval over permission-filtered documents and show citations. Measure accuracy on the evaluation set before a pilot, then log real usage and review failures weekly.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an AI feature before deploying it at a client?
questions.a: Build a labelled set from real client cases that includes hard and edge cases. Define metrics that match the task, such as exact field accuracy or a graded rubric. Run every prompt or model change against the set. Then run a limited pilot with human review and compare with the current process.

questions.q: How do you reduce hallucinations in a client deployment?
questions.a: Ground the model in retrieved client data and require it to cite sources. Allow it to answer that it does not know. Constrain outputs to a schema where possible, validate them in code, and keep a human review step for high-impact outputs. Monitor with sampled audits.

questions.q: How do you make an AI agent safe to take actions in client systems?
questions.a: Give it narrow tools with least-privilege credentials, validate every tool input, and require human approval for actions that change records or send messages. Log each step, set limits on spend and number of actions, and test with adversarial inputs including instructions hidden in documents.

questions.q: When would you choose rules over a model?
questions.a: When the logic is simple and known, when every decision must be explainable, or when there is no labelled data yet. Rules ship quickly, build user trust and produce the labels a model needs later. I move to a model when rules stop improving and I have a baseline to beat.

questions.q: How do you handle data privacy with LLMs at an enterprise client?
questions.a: Confirm where the model runs and what the provider retains. Keep data inside approved regions and accounts, mask personal data that the task does not need, and enforce the asking user's permissions at retrieval time. Get security and legal sign-off on the data flow before any pilot.

questions.q: How do you staff and sequence a twelve-week engagement with two engineers?
questions.a: Both do discovery together in the first two weeks so context is shared. Then one leads data and pipelines and the other the application, with daily syncing. I keep one weekly goal, schedule security and access work in week one, and reserve the last two weeks for handover.

questions.q: How do you decide to end or pause an engagement?
questions.a: If after discovery there is no sponsor, no measurable problem or no access to data, I say so and recommend a pause with clear conditions to restart. Continuing without those wastes both sides' money and damages trust.

questions.q: How do you grow a junior FDE?
questions.a: Pair them on client meetings first, then let them run one with me present. Give them ownership of a bounded piece with a real user. Review their written updates as carefully as their code, and debrief after every difficult client moment.

questions.q: How do you turn one successful use case into account growth?
questions.a: Publish the result in the sponsor's own terms, with the metric. Ask who else has a similar problem and get an introduction. Pick a second use case that reuses the data already integrated, so it is faster and shows the platform effect.
